options.text: The slow weathering of rock at the surface
The shaking of the ground from a sudden release of energy in Earth's crust
A crack that forms only at ancient fault lines
The melting of rock deep inside the mantle

items.explanation: An earthquake is the shaking of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy that has built up in Earth's crust.

items.stem: Stressed rock bends for years, then fractures and snaps back toward its original shape. What is this process called?

options.text: Elastic rebound
Differentiation
Convection
Erosion

items.explanation: Elastic rebound is when stressed rock releases its stored energy, fractures, and returns toward its original shape. That released energy causes the shaking.

items.stem: Where does the energy that an earthquake releases come from?

options.text: Heat from the Sun warming the surface
Rain soaking into the soil
Stress that slowly builds up in rock as plates move
The pull of the Moon's gravity

items.explanation: Moving plates put stress on rock along faults. The rock bends and stores energy over time, sometimes for hundreds of years, until it fractures.

items.stem: What is the focus of an earthquake?

options.text: The point on the surface where shaking is strongest
The fastest seismic wave
The instrument that records the quake
The point inside Earth where the earthquake begins

items.explanation: The focus is the point inside Earth where an earthquake begins and the stored energy is first released.

items.stem: A news report gives the location of an earthquake on a map. Which point is it most likely describing?

options.text: The epicenter, on the surface above the focus
The focus, deep underground
The fault zone in the mantle
The magnitude scale reading

items.explanation: The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above the focus. Because it is a surface location, it is the point people can mark on a map.

items.stem: A reverse fault forms where one block of rock is pushed up and over another. At which plate boundary does this happen?

options.text: A transform boundary
A divergent boundary
A convergent boundary
It does not happen at any boundary

items.explanation: Reverse faults form at convergent boundaries, where plates push together and the squeezing force drives one block up over the other.

items.stem: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other. Which type of fault does this create?

options.text: A normal fault
A strike-slip fault
A reverse fault
No fault at all

items.explanation: A strike-slip fault forms at a transform boundary, where blocks of rock grind sideways past each other instead of moving up or down.

items.stem: Which statement correctly compares P waves and S waves?

options.text: S waves are faster and travel through liquids
P waves and S waves are exactly the same
P waves travel through solids only
P waves are faster and can travel through solids, liquids, and gases

items.explanation: P waves are the fastest seismic waves and travel through solids, liquids, and gases. S waves are slower and travel through solids only.

items.stem: Two earthquakes have the same magnitude, but one causes far more damage. What best explains the difference?

options.text: The more damaging quake had a higher intensity because of where it struck
Magnitude and damage are always identical
The less damaging quake had a higher magnitude
Intensity measures the strength of the quake itself

items.explanation: Magnitude measures the strength of the quake, while intensity measures its effects on people and places. The same magnitude can cause very different intensity depending on where it hits.

items.stem: Which sequence correctly traces how stored energy becomes shaking at the surface?

options.text: Seismic waves form first, then stress builds, then rock bends
Stress bends rock, the rock rebounds at the focus, and seismic waves shake the surface
The epicenter releases energy that travels down to the focus
Rain weakens rock, which then melts and erupts

items.explanation: Stress slowly bends rock and stores energy. The rock fractures and rebounds at the focus, releasing energy as seismic waves that travel out and shake the surface near the epicenter.
